interview_metadata.name: Sherry Kirkus
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised here in northern Idaho, not far from Spirit Lake, in a family where you were expected to help, keep your word, and not make too much fuss. My dad worked around timber and farm equipment, and my mother kept the household running but also took seasonal work when money was tight. I was the oldest daughter, so I learned early how to stretch groceries, watch younger siblings, weed a garden row straight, and get everybody to church on time Sunday morning. After high school I took some classes at North Idaho College, mostly bookkeeping and office skills, but I married my husband, Leonard, before I finished a degree. We built a life that was modest but steady: raising two children, keeping a garden, helping at church suppers, and making sure bills were paid even when his work hours changed with the season. I was a homemaker for many years, though I always felt like that meant being the scheduler, bookkeeper, cook, nurse, and repair person all in one. As the children got older, I volunteered more, first at church as treasurer and then at the library and senior center, where I now help coordinate activities. The biggest events in my life have been marriage, motherhood, caring for aging parents, losing my father, and learning that I could still be useful and needed after the children were grown.

follow_ups.question: What is one childhood memory that still feels very clear to you?
follow_ups.response: I remember standing in my mother's kitchen in late August, steam on the windows from canning tomatoes, and being handed a clean towel to wipe jar rims. It was hot and repetitive, but there was comfort in knowing exactly what each person was supposed to do.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped you the most when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My mother shaped my habits the most. She was not sentimental, but she was steady, and she taught me that taking care of people usually looks like doing the small jobs before anyone has to ask.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The clearest crossroads was when I left school and chose marriage and home life instead of finishing college. I had taken classes in bookkeeping and thought maybe I could work in an office in Coeur d'Alene, but Leonard and I were serious, and in those days it felt natural to start a household. I do not regret marrying him, but I sometimes wonder what I might have done with a degree. Later, when the children were grown, I reached another crossroads: whether to stay only at home or step into volunteering more publicly. Becoming church treasurer and then helping at the senior center gave me confidence, because I realized the skills I had used privately for decades were real skills. That decision shaped this stage of my life a great deal.

follow_ups.question: What made the senior center feel like the right place to put your energy?
follow_ups.response: It was practical and close to home, and the seniors needed dependable people more than fancy people. I liked that I could make a calendar, call volunteers, check supplies, and see the result right away.

follow_ups.question: Do you still think about the office work path you mentioned?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, mostly when I am balancing accounts or using spreadsheets. I think I would have been good at it, but I also know my family needed me when they did.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a mix. Marrying Leonard felt like a conscious choice, but leaving college happened gradually as wedding plans, money, and family expectations all lined up in that direction.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone advise you strongly one way or another?
follow_ups.response: My mother said a woman should know how to support herself, but she also thought marriage was important. She did not push hard either way.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about that choice now?
follow_ups.response: Peaceful most days. I carry a little curiosity, but not bitterness.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, I think better advising at the college or a small scholarship might have helped me see a way to continue part time. Back then I did not know how to ask for that kind of help.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have made the biggest difference?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting down with me and showing a realistic schedule and cost plan. I respond well when I can see things written out.

follow_ups.question: Would you encourage a young woman now to finish school?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if she can. Even a certificate gives a person more options.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Leonard Kirkus, and we have been married over forty years. He is a quiet man, handy with tools, and more relaxed than I am, which is probably good for both of us. We have two grown children. Our daughter, Melanie, lives in Coeur d'Alene and works in a medical office; she calls me usually on Sunday afternoons. Our son, Brian, is over near Spokane with his wife and two children, and we see them about once a month if weather and schedules cooperate. My grandchildren are a great joy to me, though I try not to hover. Family is very important, but I also believe grown children need room to run their own homes.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Leonard do together in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: We have breakfast together most mornings, watch the evening news, and usually drive into town together for groceries on Wednesdays. On Saturdays he may work in the shop while I am in the garden, but we check in all day.

follow_ups.question: How do you stay connected with your grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: I mail cards, send short texts through their parents, and knit them things they may or may not wear. When they visit, I like baking apple crumble with them because it gives us something to do with our hands.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Linda, who lives in Sandpoint, and a brother, Carl, in Montana. Linda and I talk often; Carl is more distant but still family.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Linda?
follow_ups.response: Usually every couple of weeks, either for coffee or when she comes through Spirit Lake.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you and Carl less close?
follow_ups.response: Mostly distance and personality. He is private, and I try not to take it personally.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, I have a small circle that matters very much. My closest friend is Marlene from church; we have known each other since our children were little, and we can sit together without filling every silence. I also have friends through the library book club, especially Joan and Patrice, and a few women from bridge who meet twice a month. At the senior center, I am friendly with several regulars, but I still think of that as service first. I am not someone with a huge social calendar, but I like dependable ties.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Marlene usually do when you get together?
follow_ups.response: Coffee at her kitchen table or mine, sometimes with a plate of muffins. We talk about church, family, recipes, and who needs help that week.

follow_ups.question: How often does the book club meet?
follow_ups.response: Once a month at the library, usually the second Thursday afternoon. We mostly read historical fiction and local history.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Spirit Lake, Idaho, in a quiet area where people know whose truck belongs in which driveway. There are trees, lake access not too far away, and enough space for my vegetable garden. It is not fancy, and some homes are newer while others have been patched and added onto over time. I like hearing birds in the morning and being able to wave to neighbors while still having privacy. The town is small enough that news travels quickly, which can be helpful or a little much depending on the news.

follow_ups.question: What places in town do you go to most often?
follow_ups.response: The library, church, the grocery store, the senior center, and the post office. Those are my regular stops.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few very well, especially the retired couple next door. With others it is more waving, checking mail, and keeping an eye out.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock doors and keep porch lights on, but I do not feel afraid walking in the morning.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Late at night if I hear unfamiliar vehicles slowing down. That is more caution than fear.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for one another?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially during winter storms or if someone has not picked up mail.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The best parts are the lake, the quiet, and the sense that people will help when it counts. The hard parts are icy roads, limited medical services nearby, and sometimes too much gossip.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when roads are icy?
follow_ups.response: I plan ahead, combine errands, and keep extra pantry staples so I do not have to drive unless necessary.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there despite the inconveniences?
follow_ups.response: Roots. My routines, church, garden, and family memories are here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just Leonard and me in the house. We have been empty nesters for many years, though the house still has a guest room with toys and extra blankets for the grandkids. Leonard takes care of heavier yard work and repairs, and I handle most meals, budgeting, appointments, and household records. We share the house comfortably, though I will admit I like things put back where they belong.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide chores day to day?
follow_ups.response: I cook, plan groceries, clean the kitchen, pay bills, and manage calendars. Leonard handles trash, mowing, snow shoveling, and repairs.

follow_ups.question: Do you have pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now. We had a dog years ago, but at this stage I like not having another responsibility.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Leonard.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: Not unless family visits for a weekend.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Our grandchildren sometimes stay for a weekend, and occasionally Linda stays overnight if weather is bad.

follow_ups.question: How often do the grandchildren stay?
follow_ups.response: Maybe three or four times a year.

follow_ups.question: Where do guests sleep?
follow_ups.response: In the small guest room at the back of the house.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is two?
follow_ups.response: Yes, two.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone recently moved out?
follow_ups.response: No, not recently.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Most mornings I get up around 6:15, make coffee, and walk near the lake if the weather is decent. Mondays I usually do household planning, laundry, and check the senior center calendar. Tuesdays and Thursdays are often volunteer days, either at the senior center or library. Wednesday is grocery and errand day with Leonard. Friday I try to keep lighter for gardening, baking, or catching up with my sister. Sundays are church, a simple lunch, and calls with the children.

follow_ups.question: How long is your morning walk?
follow_ups.response: About thirty to forty minutes. I keep a steady pace but do not push hard.

follow_ups.question: When do you do your gardening?
follow_ups.response: Usually late morning or early evening in warm months, after the dew dries or when the heat has passed.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not work for pay anymore. My work now is volunteer work, mainly coordinating activities for the senior center and helping at the county library. At the senior center I help put together activity calendars, call people to confirm who is bringing what, and make sure supplies are purchased within budget. At the library I shelve books and sometimes help set up the meeting room for book club. It is not employment, but it gives structure to my week and makes me feel useful.

follow_ups.question: How many hours a week do you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Usually six to ten hours, depending on whether there is an event coming up.

follow_ups.question: What senior center activity takes the most planning?
follow_ups.response: The monthly lunch-and-program days. Food, seating, rides, sign-up sheets, and cleanup all have to be accounted for.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the household budget in a binder and update it every Friday morning. I also maintain a recipe journal, a garden notebook, and a birdwatching log. I help Marlene get to appointments sometimes, and I check on an older neighbor if we have bad weather. During church bake sales I usually make jam or apple crumble and help count donations afterward.

follow_ups.question: What is in your household budget binder?
follow_ups.response: Monthly bills, receipts, medical statements, grocery totals, and a running list of upcoming expenses.

follow_ups.question: What do you track in your bird log?
follow_ups.response: Date, weather, species, where I saw it, and sometimes a note like first robin of spring.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is that Leonard has needed more help keeping track of medical appointments and medications. Nothing dramatic, but enough that I added a weekly pillbox check and a calendar reminder system. I have also been trying to walk earlier in the morning because my knees feel better when I move before sitting too long. At the senior center, we recently added a Tuesday craft hour, so I am there more regularly now.

follow_ups.question: How do you organize Leonard's appointments?
follow_ups.response: I write them on the kitchen calendar, put reminders in my phone, and keep papers in a labeled folder.

follow_ups.question: What happens during craft hour?
follow_ups.response: Mostly simple projects like cards, knitting, or seasonal decorations. I make sure there are supplies and enough chairs.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown now, so I do not have school-age children at home. When Melanie and Brian were young, mornings were lunches packed, school bus timing, chores before they left, and homework at the kitchen table after school. Melanie liked reading and choir, while Brian played some baseball and helped Leonard with outdoor projects. Now I hear about my grandchildren's school routines more than I manage them.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with the grandchildren's school activities?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally, like attending a concert or helping with a baked good if their parents ask.

follow_ups.question: What did you expect from your children after school when they were young?
follow_ups.response: Homework first, then chores, then free time. That was the order in our house.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited and mostly ordinary. I have had one speeding warning years ago and have called the sheriff's office about a suspicious vehicle near a neighbor's place. In a small town, you may know officers through school events, church drives, or community safety talks. I tend to be respectful of law enforcement, but I also think every profession needs accountability.

follow_ups.question: What happened with the suspicious vehicle?
follow_ups.response: It turned out to be someone looking for a driveway address, but the deputy called back, which I appreciated.

follow_ups.question: Do you interact with police at community events?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes at safety presentations for seniors or during town events where they help with traffic.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The main ones are when officers came to the senior center to talk about phone scams and elder fraud. That was useful because several people I know have gotten suspicious calls.

follow_ups.question: Did you change anything after that talk?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became more careful about unknown numbers and reminded Leonard not to give information over the phone.

follow_ups.question: Do you share that advice with others?
follow_ups.response: I do, especially with seniors who live alone.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and neither has Leonard or our children. I have known acquaintances over the years who had DUIs, but nobody in my immediate family.

follow_ups.question: Did those acquaintances' experiences affect your views?
follow_ups.response: They made me think consequences matter, but so does helping people get back on track.

follow_ups.question: Was alcohol involved in most of those cases?
follow_ups.response: The ones I knew about, yes, mostly drinking and driving.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in nearly every election, including local ones. I was raised to think voting is part of being a responsible citizen, and local races can affect roads, schools, libraries, and taxes directly. I usually read the voter pamphlet, talk with Leonard, and sometimes ask people I trust if they know a candidate personally. I do not put signs in the yard very often, but I do show up to vote.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually in person if the weather is fine. I like the routine of going to the polling place.

follow_ups.question: Which local issues matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Library funding, senior services, road maintenance, property taxes, and emergency services.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as moderate conservative, with a practical streak. I believe in personal responsibility, careful spending, and not expanding government just because something sounds nice. At the same time, I support local programs that clearly help people, like senior transportation, libraries, volunteer fire services, and food drives. I am not comfortable with the mean tone politics has taken, and I do not like people acting as if everyone on the other side is foolish or evil. I tend to vote Republican more often, especially on fiscal issues, but I look at the person in local races. If someone is honest, competent, and cares about the town, that matters more to me than a party label.

follow_ups.question: What does careful spending mean to you in local government?
follow_ups.response: Clear budgets, no wasteful projects, and being honest about taxes before approving something. I like seeing where the money will go.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever voted for a Democrat?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in a local race when I knew the person and trusted her judgment. I am more flexible locally than nationally.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less patient with loud party fighting and more interested in whether people can actually govern. I still lean conservative, but I am more willing than I used to be to support local measures if I can see the benefit. The pandemic years also made me think more about how fragile older people can be and how important clear public information is. I do not feel like my basic values changed, but I pay more attention to tone and competence now.

follow_ups.question: What kind of tone turns you away from a candidate?
follow_ups.response: Mocking, name-calling, or acting like compromise is weakness. I do not trust that.

follow_ups.question: What local measure did you support recently?
follow_ups.response: I supported a library levy because I use the library and see how many families and seniors depend on it.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say they affected me somewhat. Spirit Lake is not very diverse, so it is easy for people here to feel removed from those conversations. But seeing the news made me think about experiences I have not had to worry about as a white woman. I also believe policing is difficult work, so I hold both thoughts: respect for officers and the belief that unfair treatment should be addressed.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it with family?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly with Melanie and my daughter-in-law. The younger ones are more direct about race than my generation tends to be.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything you read or watched?
follow_ups.response: I tried to read more than just headlines, including a few library articles and interviews.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raised real concerns about whether everyone is treated the same under the law. I do not always agree with every protest tactic or slogan, but I try not to dismiss the pain behind it. My instinct is to ask what concrete changes would help: better training, body cameras, hiring standards, and consequences when someone abuses authority. I also think small communities should listen before assuming the issue has nothing to do with them.

follow_ups.question: What kind of reform sounds reasonable to you?
follow_ups.response: Training, de-escalation, clear complaint processes, and removing officers who have repeated serious problems.

follow_ups.question: What makes you cautious about the movement?
follow_ups.response: When protests turn destructive or when the message sounds like all police are bad. That is where I pull back.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking that race is something many white people my age were taught not to talk about, as if being polite solved it. I do not think I grew up hateful, but I did grow up in a place where there were very few people of color and very little honest conversation about history. Reading historical fiction and local history has made me more aware that whose story gets told matters. I still feel clumsy talking about it, but I am trying to listen more.

follow_ups.question: Has anything you read stood out?
follow_ups.response: Books about westward settlement and Native communities have made me think about land and history differently.

follow_ups.question: Do people in your circle discuss race often?
follow_ups.response: Not often. When it comes up, people tend to get careful or defensive.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked quietly with family and a couple of friends. I have not joined protests, but I have tried to be more thoughtful and less quick to dismiss people who say they have been mistreated.

follow_ups.question: Who have you talked with most openly?
follow_ups.response: Melanie, because she reads more current news and challenges me without being disrespectful.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any civic action because of it?
follow_ups.response: Mostly paying closer attention to sheriff and local law enforcement races.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Leonard is more skeptical and tends to say people should obey the law and things would go better. Melanie is more concerned about systemic unfairness. My church friends vary; some avoid the subject, and some say the country needs more respect in every direction. I often feel like I am in the middle, trying to keep conversations from becoming arguments.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep those conversations calm?
follow_ups.response: I ask people to be specific and lower their voices. I also change the subject if it turns into repeating slogans.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone close to you attended protests?
follow_ups.response: Not that I know of. My family discusses things more than demonstrates.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For 65, I would say my health is decent but not perfect. I have mild arthritis in my knees and hands, and my blood pressure runs a little high if I do not watch salt and stress. I walk most mornings, garden, and try to cook real food instead of too many packaged things. My hands can ache after knitting too long, and I have to pace myself with heavier chores. Overall I am grateful, but I pay more attention than I used to.

follow_ups.question: Do you take regular medication?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a blood pressure medication and occasional over-the-counter pain reliever for arthritis.

follow_ups.question: What helps your knees most?
follow_ups.response: Walking regularly, stretching, sensible shoes, and not kneeling too long in the garden.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I live where walking and gardening are natural parts of life. It is harder in winter when roads are slick and I am tempted to stay inside and bake. Health care distance can also be a challenge because appointments in Coeur d'Alene take planning. Stress makes it harder too; when I worry, I snack or lose sleep.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you try to eat for health?
follow_ups.response: Vegetable soups, salads from the garden, oatmeal, apples, and smaller portions of meat.

follow_ups.question: What tends to throw you off?
follow_ups.response: Holidays, bad weather, and weeks with too many appointments.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The biggest thing was being told my blood pressure needed medication instead of just diet changes. That worried me at first because I do not like adding pills, but it has been manageable. I also had a bad arthritis flare in my right hand last winter that made knitting and jar opening difficult for a few weeks. No broken bones or hospital stays, thankfully. I had my regular screenings and try to keep up with them.

follow_ups.question: How did you react to starting blood pressure medicine?
follow_ups.response: I asked a lot of questions and wrote down the dosage and side effects. Once I saw better numbers, I calmed down.

follow_ups.question: Did the hand pain change your routines?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I limited knitting to shorter sessions and used Leonard's help with stubborn jars.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health does not stop me from volunteering or caring for the household, but it slows me down sometimes. I plan heavier work earlier in the day and leave space to rest if my knees or hands act up.

follow_ups.question: Have you cancelled commitments because of health?
follow_ups.response: Rarely, but I have traded tasks with another volunteer if I knew standing too long would bother me.

follow_ups.question: What household task is hardest physically?
follow_ups.response: Deep cleaning floors and lifting heavy garden supplies.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, Leonard's health is more on my mind lately. He has some back trouble and needs monitoring for cholesterol and blood pressure. I also helped care for my mother before she passed, so I know how quickly caregiving can become a full schedule. Right now Leonard is independent, but I keep track of appointments and medications because I want to stay ahead of problems.

follow_ups.question: What caregiving tasks do you do for Leonard?
follow_ups.response: Mostly reminders, paperwork, appointment scheduling, and making sure meals are not too salty.

follow_ups.question: Does caregiving worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because I know one fall or diagnosis can change everything quickly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have not gone without major care, but we have delayed things when the cost or travel felt like too much. Specialist appointments can mean driving to Coeur d'Alene or Spokane, and that takes coordination. Medicare helps, and we have supplemental coverage, but dental and glasses still add up. I keep a folder for medical bills so nothing slips through, because that is one place mistakes get expensive.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed?
follow_ups.response: Dental work once, and Leonard delayed a physical therapy appointment because of cost and winter roads.

follow_ups.question: Who helps you understand medical bills?
follow_ups.response: Mostly I do it myself, but Melanie helps if a statement is confusing.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like that. I use home remedies in the old-fashioned sense: tea with honey, heating pads, Epsom salt soaks, and homemade soup when someone is sick. Leonard has seen a chiropractor for his back a few times. I believe in doctors, but I also think comfort care at home has its place for minor things.

follow_ups.question: Do you use herbal supplements?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. I might drink peppermint or chamomile tea, but I am cautious about pills and supplements.

follow_ups.question: Did chiropractic care help Leonard?
follow_ups.response: A little for stiffness, but he still has to stretch and be careful lifting.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke and never have. I might have a glass of wine at a holiday meal or a small drink at a wedding, but alcohol is not my way of coping. When I am upset, I am more likely to clean a drawer, make soup, walk, pray, or knit. I can overdo sweets when stressed, especially if I have been baking.

follow_ups.question: When was the last time you had alcohol?
follow_ups.response: Probably a small glass of wine at Thanksgiving dinner.

follow_ups.question: What coping habit works best?
follow_ups.response: Walking first thing in the morning. It gets the worry moving instead of circling in my head.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or anything like that. I take my prescribed blood pressure medicine as directed, and for pain I use ibuprofen or acetaminophen occasionally. The most recent time was after a long afternoon weeding, when my hands and knees were sore, so I took one dose after dinner and used a heating pad. I am careful because I do not want to rely on pain pills casually.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep medication organized?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I use a weekly pill organizer and keep a medication list in my purse.

follow_ups.question: Why avoid marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Partly habit and partly caution. It is just not something I am comfortable with.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We rely on Medicare, supplemental insurance, and careful budgeting. I set aside money each month for copays, prescriptions, dental, and glasses because those expenses are predictable even if the exact amount changes. We use generic prescriptions when possible. I also compare statements against the insurance notices, because I have caught billing errors before.

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs strain the budget?
follow_ups.response: They can, especially dental or specialist visits, but planning keeps it from becoming a crisis most months.

follow_ups.question: Do you use any discount programs?
follow_ups.response: We have used pharmacy discount pricing when it is cheaper than insurance.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally in favor of vaccines, especially for older adults. I get my flu shot and COVID boosters when my doctor recommends them, though I still ask questions about timing and side effects.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about COVID vaccination?
follow_ups.response: At first I wondered how fast it came together, but my doctor explained the risks clearly.

follow_ups.question: Does Leonard feel the same?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though he grumbles more about appointments than I do.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary doctor is my main source. I also trust the pharmacist in town, official health department information, and sometimes Melanie because she works in a medical office and can help me sort out what is reliable. I do not trust random Facebook posts, especially ones with dramatic headlines. If something sounds alarming, I wait and check before passing it along.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide whether an article is trustworthy?
follow_ups.response: I look for who published it, whether a doctor or public health agency is cited, and whether it sounds balanced.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever share vaccine information online?
follow_ups.response: Almost never. I would rather talk one-on-one if someone asks.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year I have felt mostly steady, but with more worry than I would like. I worry about Leonard's health, rising costs, and whether I am keeping up with everything I promised to do. I also feel grateful because I have family, church, the garden, and meaningful volunteer work. My mood improves when I have a plan and a written list. I get unsettled when too many things are uncertain or when people depend on me and I am afraid of missing something.

follow_ups.question: What does worry feel like in your day?
follow_ups.response: It shows up as checking things twice, waking early, or making lists when I should be relaxing.

follow_ups.question: What has brought you the most peace recently?
follow_ups.response: Morning walks, prayer, and seeing the garden come up in neat rows.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last winter Leonard had a spell of back pain and we had two medical appointments, a furnace repair, and a senior center luncheon all in the same week. I remember sitting at the kitchen table with bills and sign-up sheets spread out, feeling like I could not keep everything straight. I snapped at Leonard over something small, which is not how I want to be. Afterward I took a walk, called Marlene, and reorganized the week into a written schedule. By Friday things were not solved, but they were manageable again.

follow_ups.question: What did Marlene say that helped?
follow_ups.response: She reminded me I could ask someone else to handle decorations for the luncheon. That sounds small, but it took a weight off.

follow_ups.question: Did you apologize to Leonard?
follow_ups.response: Yes, after dinner. He said he knew I was overloaded, but I still needed to say it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would not say I have depression, but I do struggle with anxiety or worry. It is not diagnosed as a disorder, but it is part of my temperament. I like order, and when things are loose or uncertain, my mind starts filling in all the ways something could go wrong. I manage it with lists, prayer, walking, and talking with people I trust.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever talked to a counselor?
follow_ups.response: No, not formally. I would consider it if things got worse, but so far I manage.

follow_ups.question: Does anxiety affect your sleep?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. I wake around 4:00 and start thinking through tasks.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My family is doing fairly well, though everyone carries stress. Melanie gets tired from medical office work, Brian worries about expenses with children, and Leonard gets frustrated when his back limits him.

follow_ups.question: Do they come to you for support?
follow_ups.response: Yes, often for practical support or just someone steady to listen.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel burdened by that role?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I also value being needed.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion is important to me, though I am not showy about it. I was raised Protestant and now attend a small community church with Baptist-leaning traditions. Sunday worship, hymns, prayer lists, and church suppers have shaped my life. I was church treasurer for years, and that taught me how much trust a congregation places in ordinary people. My faith is practical: visit the sick, take food to a family, keep promises, and admit when you fall short. I do have questions like anyone, but church gives me rhythm and community.

follow_ups.question: How often do you attend church?
follow_ups.response: Most Sundays, unless weather or illness gets in the way.

follow_ups.question: What church activities do you still help with?
follow_ups.response: Bake sales, meal trains, donation counting, and sometimes organizing volunteers for seasonal drives.

follow_ups.question: What local Facebook groups do you follow?

follow_ups.question: Do you comment on political posts?
follow_ups.response: Almost never. I have learned it rarely improves anything.

transcript.response: I would not ask for personal support on Facebook. If I need help, I call family, Marlene, or someone at church directly.

follow_ups.question: Would you respond if someone else asked for help online?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if I knew them or the need was confirmed through church or a trusted person.

follow_ups.question: Have you donated through social media fundraisers?
follow_ups.response: Once or twice, but usually I prefer local, direct giving.

transcript.response: My stress has gone up some because of health appointments and prices. I am trying to cope by saying no sooner, delegating more at the senior center, and not checking news late at night.

follow_ups.question: What have you said no to recently?
follow_ups.response: I declined to lead an extra holiday committee and agreed only to help with the sign-up sheet.

follow_ups.question: Does avoiding news at night help?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I sleep better if I read a book instead.

follow_ups.question: How often do you add to savings?
follow_ups.response: Monthly if nothing unusual has happened, even if it is a small amount.

follow_ups.response: My parents, especially my mother. She could make five dollars act like ten.

follow_ups.question: How much do you like to keep available?
follow_ups.response: I feel best with at least a few months of basic expenses, though we are not always exactly there.

transcript.response: We do not have student loans or a mortgage. We use a credit card for convenience but pay it off monthly. We have no family loans right now, and I would work hard to keep it that way.

follow_ups.question: What did you postpone most recently?
follow_ups.response: A dental crown consultation and a new pair of walking shoes for a few weeks.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help financially?
follow_ups.response: No. We managed by adjusting the budget.

transcript.response: I was primarily a homemaker, and now I would describe myself as retired from paid work but active as a volunteer coordinator.
